If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

87:It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract`, `test` and `override`. It refuses an `override` of or by a method with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile an override of or by a method with static parameters of its own yet.' It also refuses one in a generic trait or object where its parameter types, or the overridden declaration's, name a static parameter: 'Can't compile an override in a trait or object with static parameters, …' (ledger row 1106). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
146:  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
166:- Where a function of no parameters is passed at a parameter of an arrow type that its own type coerces to, as a `() -> ZZ32` at `() -> ZZ64`, the program dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` when the callee calls it (ledger row 1084). At one parameter, the coercion runs. Declare the function at the parameter's arrow type.

- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.

## Building

Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.

- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` and `default_repository/caches-one`, each if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
- `ant cleanCache` deletes both folders, whatever their stamp.
- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.

## After an edit of the library

The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.

- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.

# Cold read of `clean.txt`

Read with only `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` and the skill's `references/` (not `revival-changes.md` or `sources.md`). Terms looked up there: the Return Type Rule and walk's load check (`interpreter.md`, "What walk checks"), the team's object-type shortcut (`interpreter.md:81`, row 697), value objects (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"), the stamp and the library order (`build-and-caches.md`), seeding (`worktrees.md`), the Working Draft (`specification.md:6`), the record's terms (`records.md`).

## 1. F-375

**Established:** Walk's check at load now applies the Return Type Rule to a pair made of a generic declaration and a plain one (no static parameters) when the plain one's domain lies inside the generic one's declared domain, even where the two parameter lists differ only at object types (where the team's old check would have called them excluding and skipped the rule). The pair loads if the plain result lies below the generic result by one of three readings, and is refused with a message naming the Return Type Rule otherwise (row 998, fixed). A tuple result is compared element by element (row 1058, fixed). Separately, `FTraitOrObject.enforceValueness` refuses a non-value type declared below a value type, and no longer refuses the symbolic type that stands for a type parameter (row 997, fixed).

**Conditions:** Walk only, at load, generic-beside-plain pairs. Limits: a plain declaration that writes no return type is not judged (row 1044); `comprises` clauses are not read; two plain declarations still get the team's shortcut (row 697). Since the five number types were merged with their objects (P-178, F-379), every generic-beside-plain pair over them goes through the declared-domain reading. Three of the choices (no `comprises` reading, no judgment without a return type, the value check and its "both directions" repair, the three readings) were made by the coordinator, the planner or a worker; the curator decided none.

**Consequence:** A worker should write the return type on a plain overload beside a generic one (otherwise the rule is silently skipped), should expect a pair over object types that breaks the rule to be refused at load now, and should treat the listed choices as open, not as the curator's decisions (if one matters to the work, that is a reason to explore). No walk test changed between loading and refusing, and no expected-failure test changed kind.

**Evidence:** The seven named tests under `ProjectFortress/tests/`; the suite result stated (every pair loaded before still loads); old-against-new runs in the three cited reports.

**Could not resolve:**
- "an own generic's declared domain": unclear wording. I read it as "a generic declaration of the same name"; it could also mean "a declaration with static parameters of its own" (F-26's term).
- "by one of three readings that the report gives": the entry does not say what the three readings are, nor at which instance "the generic's" result is taken. So I cannot tell from the entry which pairs load. Not standing alone.
- "a `comprises` clause is not read (row 550's pair at `ZZ64`, fixed since `ZZ64` is an object, F-379)": two readings. Either row 550 is an example of the limitation that no longer bites because `ZZ64` stopped needing a `comprises` clause, or row 550 is where `comprises` reading was fixed. I took the first; the wording does not settle it.
- "the repair of both directions in one step": unclear wording. Both directions of what: of the value check (refusing a non-value below a value type, and passing a type parameter), or of the Return Type Rule (loading and refusing)?
- "the five number types merged with their objects": a history/language concept I lack. The skill says the number types other than `QQ` are object types (`interpreter.md:78`) and that the prelude has seven number types each one `value object` (`compiler.md:34`); neither says which five, or what they were merged from.
- "passes the symbolic type of a type parameter": where such a type meets the value check is not said; the test names (`...ValueBoundWalk`) suggest a type parameter bounded by a value type. Unclear wording.
- "the coordinator", "the batch's planner": roles the skill does not define; only their consequence (not the curator) matters, and that is clear.
- Conflict with the skill: `interpreter.md:80` still says walk refuses row 1058's valid tuple pair, which this entry says is fixed. A worker reading both meets two contrary statements.

## 2. F-403

**Established:** The one library declares `EQV` (`≡`) and `NEQV` (`≢`) on two `Boolean`s as top-level operators next to `<->`. `EQV` is `if a then b else NOT b end` (deliberately avoiding `=`, which row 994 concerns on the compiled path), and `NEQV` is `NOT (a EQV b)`, as the specification defines `≢`. Both paths run them under the one library. Applied to two objects of a program's own type they are type errors: walk stops at the call with a unification error, the compiled checker refuses the call.

**Conditions:** One library, both paths. The specification and the prelude make them methods of `Boolean`; the one library keeps top-level operators for its boolean operators. With `AplCore` imported, its infix `≡` and prefix `≢` over `RR64` and arrays share an overload set with the library's two: its calls give what they gave before, and booleans get the library's answers (`t ≡ f` is `false`, `t ≢ f` is `true`). No gated program and no microGPT line imports `AplCore`. Limits: an undeclared equivalence operator such as `APPROX` still loads under walk and fails at the call with an internal error (row 1118); `⊕`, `⊼`, `⊽` and `majority` are not declared (row 1121).

**Consequence:** A worker can use `≡`/`≢` on booleans under the one library on both paths, should not expect them to work on other types, and should know that the top-level form and the merge with `AplCore` are plan defaults the curator has not decided. Avoid `=` on two booleans in compiled code (row 994).

**Evidence:** `tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`, `one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`; the quoted error messages; the cited report sections.

**Could not resolve:**
- "within P-37, a default of the batch's plan that the curator has not decided": two readings. Since a P- entry is a curator's decision (`records.md`), I read it as "the top-level form fits within P-37, and is itself a plan default"; read literally, it says P-37 is undecided.
- "This also is the plan's default, not decided by the curator": unclear what "this" is: the merging with `AplCore`'s operators into one overload set, or the absence of any conflict handling, or the fact that nothing gated imports `AplCore`.
- "(row 994 is `=` of two booleans, compiled)": telegraphic. I read it as "row 994 is an open defect of `=` on two booleans on the compiled path", but the entry does not say the row is open or what the defect is.
- "an equivalence operator that nothing declares": a language concept (the specification's class of equivalence operators) not in the skill; the example `APPROX` lets me guess.
- "its own form for the boolean operators": inferred as "top-level operators rather than methods of `Boolean`" from the contrast; not stated.

## 3. F-404

**Established:** `seed-worktree.sh` copies `ProjectFortress/build` but not `ProjectFortress/build-one`. The implementation stamp covers `build-one` too. So when the base build has a `build-one`, the seeded worktree's stamp check fails at the first `ant` target: it prints 'Sources and build as the last build left them? no', rebuilds the Scala, and empties both `caches` and `caches-one`. Before that first build, a compiled run with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` fails with 'java.lang.Error: The type ZZ of the library that the compiled path reads is not compiled over ... FZZ ...'.

**Conditions:** Only for a worktree seeded from a base build that has `build-one`. Holds until the script is changed.

**Consequence:** A seeded worker must budget a Scala build plus the library order before the first compiled run, and should not trust a compiled one-library run in a freshly seeded worktree before building. The skill's promise that a seeded worktree "runs walk and the compiled path right away" and that `ant compileAll` "keeps the seeded caches" (`worktrees.md:36`, `:45`) does not hold in this case.

**Evidence:** `build.xml:400-402`, `:469-470` (the stamp), `seed-worktree.sh:86-93` (the copy); no test, but the command `cd ProjectFortress && FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ../bin/fortress run OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence` exits 1 with the error, in a fresh seeded worktree; report section "Defects, and their homes".

**Could not resolve:**
- `build-one`: not defined anywhere I may read. I guess it is a build output for the one library's runtime, but I cannot say what it holds or when a base build has one. Concept I lack (the skill mentions only `ProjectFortress/build`).
- "a compiled run under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` before it stops, '...'": garden-path wording. I read "before it" as "before that first build", and "stops" as the verb; it could be misread as "before it stops".
- Whether a compiled run without the variable, or a walk run, also fails before the first build is not said.
- Whether the defect has a ledger row, or is to be fixed in the script, is not said ("No test" only).

## 4. F-405

**Established:** Under walk, a trait or object can declare several generic dotted methods of one name, and walk runs them. The object builds each generic method as one symbolic instance, keyed by the method's name and the kinds of its static parameters; an object's redeclaration of a trait's generic method thus replaces it. A call without static arguments infers them and dispatches among the instances; a call with static arguments instantiates each method whose static parameters (number and kinds) accept them, then chooses by the arguments as for a top-level generic function.

**Conditions:** Walk only, dotted generic methods. Limits: two methods of the same arity whose static parameters differ only in bounds collapse into one instance and the first met is kept, so a call can silently run the less specific one (row 1125: `Nested.tk(n)` on a `ZZ32` answers 2 from `tk[\U extends Number\]` instead of 3 from `tk[\U extends ZZ32\]`). A call on a receiver "assumed at the trait" stops (row 1126). A plain and a generic method of one name: a call with static arguments stops (row 744). Of two generic functional methods of one name and arity, the second is never chosen (row 1123).

**Consequence:** A worker can overload generic dotted methods by arity and by static-parameter kinds under walk, but must not overload them only by bounds, must not mix a plain and a generic method of one name where calls write static arguments, and must not rely on the second of two same-arity generic functional methods.

**Evidence:** The first-met rule was read in the code; row 1125 was observed; tests `tests/GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss`, `GenericMethodOverloadSetWalk.fss`, `GenericOverloadStaticArgKindsWalk.fss`; the cited report sections and `SKEPTIC.md`.

**Could not resolve:**
- "one symbolic instantiation for each name and kinds of static parameters" against "Two such methods of one number of parameters ... share that instantiation": unclear whether the number of value parameters is part of the key. If it is not, two methods of different arities with the same static-parameter kinds would collide, which the arity test suggests they do not.
- "the first met is kept": first in source order, in inheritance order, or in a hash order? Not said.
- "A call on a receiver assumed at the trait stops (row 1126)": unclear wording. Walk has no static types, so I cannot tell what "assumed at the trait" means (a call on `self` in the trait's body? a receiver bound through a trait-typed variable?), nor with what error it stops.
- Conflict with the skill: `interpreter.md:82` says two generic dotted methods that differ in arity load and a call fails (row 1057). This entry's title and its `GenericMethodOverloadArity.fss` test suggest that is fixed, but the entry does not name row 1057.

## 5. F-406

**Established:** On the compiled path, a setter call `c.t := v` (a method call after the desugarer) now passes `v` at the setter's parameter type for the receiver's instance, including when the receiver is typed by a type variable whose bounds have the setter (with a cast when it has `self`'s type, F-377). When the checker leaves a call with several candidate declarations, the code generator now writes into the class the overload (dispatch) method that the call names, and, where the call's signature differs from the overload set's principal member, a forwarding method at the call's signature. So setter assignments at a narrower value, `s.r := self` at a listed type, `num(R)` beside a trait's `num(self)`, calls on `self` in such a trait, and calls that one declaration takes directly and another by coercion all compile and run; the one library's `FortressLibrary` now holds `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}`.

**Conditions:** Compiled path. The written overload method is a plan default and the forwarder a worker's choice; the alternative was routing each call through the trait; the curator has decided neither. Limit: the checker still refuses a comprised object's functional method declared at a narrower return type (row 1127).

**Consequence:** A worker can rely on these call forms compiling, should treat the generated overload method and forwarder as provisional designs, and should not write a narrower return type on a comprised object's functional method.

**Evidence:** `compiler_tests/VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun`, `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject`, `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, `CoercionAnyOverloadRungC`; the named `CodeGen` methods; report sections 1 and 5.

**Could not resolve:**
- "an arrowless call after the desugarer", "the call's arrow": compiled-path concept I lack. I guess the arrow is the function type the checker attaches to a call, and the desugared setter call has none, but the skill does not say.
- "its set split with its principal member": unclear wording and an undefined concept. I cannot tell what "principal member" is (the most general declaration? the first?) or what splitting the set means.
- "cast below self's trait where it has self's type (F-377)": unclear which value is cast to what, and what "has self's type" means here.
- "`s.r := self` at a listed type": I guess "listed" means listed in a `comprises` clause; not said.
- "`numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}`": notation I cannot read (generated method names? overload-set names?), and why it matters is not said.
- Conflict with the skill: `compiler.md:172` still lists `num(R)` for an object a `comprises` clause lists as refused (row 815); this entry says it now runs compiled.
